title: Building Bridges: Establishing a Dialogue Between Software Engineering Research and Computational Science
extended_summary:
This paper is a position piece arguing that computational science and engineering (CSE) should engage more deeply with software engineering (SE) research to improve the development, maintenance, and use of scientific software. The authors frame the problem as a long-standing disconnect between CSE and the SE research community, which has limited the transfer of evidence-based practices into scientific software development.

Rather than studying a specific intervention, the paper lays out three ways the CSE community could benefit from SE research: translating established SE methods and findings into CSE, partnering with SE researchers on topics already studied in software engineering, and helping define evidence-based practices in emerging domains such as machine learning, quantum computing, and heterogeneous computing architectures. The discussion emphasizes tools and methods such as program analysis, repository mining, case studies, and controlled experiments, but these are presented as candidate approaches rather than as evaluated interventions.

The paper is not an empirical study of a population or educational setting; it focuses on the software science and HPC/scientific computing community, particularly researchers and practitioners at national laboratories and related CSE teams. Its main conclusion is that closer collaboration with SE researchers could improve productivity, quality, and sustainability in scientific software development, and that national labs are well-positioned to lead this effort.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/opinion workshop paper about software engineering and computational science, not an empirical study of an educational AI intervention. It contains no study design, no participant sample, and no outcome evaluation relevant to K-12 learning.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured impact on student outcomes, science instruction, or educational technology use. The paper is adjacent background only and provides no evidence of effect size or intervention benefit.
